title: Police Surveillance Software Is Growing, and Experts Are Debating It
summary:
Across the United States, hundreds of police departments have real-time crime centers. These are central hubs where officers can watch and combine information from many sources at once. Many of these centers are now powered by artificial intelligence (AI) software, such as a tool called Fusus from the company Axon.

Fusus pulls together video and data from police body cameras, police car cameras, 911 calls, gunshot detectors and surveillance cameras. Sometimes it also includes cameras from private businesses that choose to take part. In 2024, just over 100 law enforcement agencies used Fusus, according to the news site 404 Media. Axon says that number has more than doubled since then.

Police officers say the tool saves time. Benjamin Weir, a captain with the Oklahoma City Police Department, said having everything in one place helps analysts work faster.

Recently, Flock cameras, which automatically read car license plates, have faced strong criticism. But privacy experts say tools like Fusus raise even bigger questions. Rachel Levinson-Waldman of New York University's Brennan Center for Justice said watching someone used to take time, staff and effort, which created natural limits. As that gets easier, she said, it becomes simpler to look at many people at once. Experts also warn the technology can sweep up innocent people by mistake.

Police told NPR they understand these worries but believe the benefits of stopping and solving crime are greater. Axon's CEO, Rick Smith, said the company values privacy and called the software "a tool to amplify human ability, not to replace human judgment."

Courts have not yet decided where the legal limits are. Law professor Andrew Guthrie Ferguson said lawmakers could set rules, such as limiting how long data is stored or requiring regular checks.
why_it_matters: Decisions about police technology affect both public safety and the privacy of everyone in a community. The rules set now could shape how much people are watched in the future.

background_read: Police departments collect information from many sources, such as cameras, emergency calls and reports from officers.
A real-time crime center is a central room where staff can see much of that information at the same time, which can help police respond faster.
In the United States, people have a right to privacy, and courts help decide when government watching goes too far.
As technology makes it easier to collect and combine data, communities debate how to balance safety and privacy.
